content.narrative_summary: Legend text explains that the SCORE chart estimates 10-year risk of fatal cardiovascular disease (CVD) in low-risk European populations based on age, gender, smoking status, systolic blood pressure, and total cholesterol. It notes that to convert fatal CVD risk to total CVD risk (fatal + non-fatal), multiply by 3 in men and 4 in women, with slight adjustments in older people. content.narrative_summary: This section defines hypertension (SBP ≥140 mmHg or DBP ≥90 mmHg) and recommends at least 30 minutes of moderate-intensity dynamic aerobic exercise (eg, walking, jogging, cycling, swimming) 5–7 days per week. Resistance training 2–3 days per week is also effective. A pre‐participation cardiovascular assessment is advised for high‐intensity sports to identify exercise‐induced symptoms and organ damage. Non‐pharmacological measures include salt and alcohol restriction, weight reduction, Mediterranean diet, smoking cessation, and tailored aerobic exercise programmes. If SBP remains >140 mmHg after 3 months, antihypertensive drugs should be started; beta-blockers and diuretics are prohibited in certain sports, while ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and calcium antagonists are preferred. Uncontrolled BP warrants restriction from competitive sports. Well‐controlled hypertensive individuals may participate in most sports except intensive power disciplines; avoid Valsalva manoeuvre and heavy isometric work. Regular follow-up and ambulatory BP assessment are recommended. High‐intensity dynamic resistance training (up to 80% 1RM with <10 repetitions) does not raise BP more than low‐intensity with ≥20 repetitions. Exaggerated BP response to exercise (eg, SBP >200 mmHg at 100 W) requires optimized medical therapy and cardiac evaluation. Young Olympic athletes may reach SBP >220 mmHg (males) or >200 mmHg (females).

content.narrative_summary: This page discusses the role of physical activity in prevention and management of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), noting that inactive individuals have a 50–80% higher risk of developing T2DM. Aerobic and resistance exercise improve glycaemic control, vascular and lipid profiles, insulin sensitivity, and reduce obesity-related complications. In pre-diabetes and metabolic syndrome, higher exercise intensity confers greater metabolic benefit. Exercise effects on muscle insulin sensitivity and coronary microvascular dysfunction in diabetes are described, including dose–response relationships and risks of exercise-induced hypoglycaemia. Recommendations emphasize combining aerobic and resistance training, daily moderate-intensity activity with supplemental balance and flexibility exercises, and undertaking cardiovascular assessment including glycaemic status and hypoglycaemia risk before engaging in high-intensity exercise. Asymptomatic diabetic individuals with normal assessments may participate in sports with caution regarding iatrogenic risks.

recommendation_tables.title: Special considerations for individuals with obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, or diabetes

rows.recommendation: In obese individuals (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 or a waist circumference > 80 cm for females or > 94 cm for males) resistance training ≥ 3 times per week, in addition to moderate or vigorous aerobic exercise (at least 30 min, 5–7 days per week) is recommended to reduce CVD risk.

In individuals with well-controlled hypertension, resistance training ≥ 3 times per week in addition to moderate or vigorous aerobic exercise (at least 30 min, 5–7 days per week) is recommended to reduce blood pressure and CVD risk.

Among individuals with diabetes mellitus, resistance training ≥ 3 times per week in addition to moderate or vigorous aerobic exercise (at least 30 min, 5–7 days per week) is recommended to improve insulin sensitivity and achieve a better CVD risk profile.
Among adults with well-controlled hypertension but high risk and/or target organ damage, high-intensity resistance exercise is not recommended.
In individuals with uncontrolled hypertension (SBP > 160 mmHg) high-intensity exercise is not recommended until blood pressure has been controlled.

section_headings: 5.2 Exercise recommendations in individuals with chronic heart failure
5.2.1 Background: rationale for exercise in chronic heart failure
content.narrative_summary:
Myocardial bridging (MB) occurs when a segment of an epicardial coronary artery, most often the left anterior descending artery, is ‘tunnelled’ under myocardium. Prevalence varies from 0.5–75% by imaging, and while traditionally benign, MB can cause ischaemia via coronary compression and a Venturi effect. Assessment focuses on anatomical characteristics and inducible ischaemia using inotropic or chronotropic stress testing; prognosis is generally good in the absence of other disease. Symptomatic patients or those with ischaemia may receive beta-blockers; coronary stenting is discouraged, and surgery considered only in select cases. Individuals with MB and evidence of ischaemia should avoid competitive sports.

In chronic heart failure (HF), exercise training is strongly recommended to improve exercise tolerance, quality of life, and reduce mortality. Before initiating exercise, contraindications (e.g., unstable cardiac disease, severe pulmonary hypertension) must be excluded, a baseline cardiological evaluation including biomarkers and preferably cardiopulmonary exercise testing should be performed, and medical therapy optimized according to guidelines, including device implantation when indicated.

content.narrative_summary: Primary mitral regurgitation (MR) is confirmed and quantified by echocardiography. Sports participation recommendations are based on symptomatic status, MR severity, LV function, systolic pulmonary artery pressure (sPAP), and exercise-induced arrhythmias. Both athletic training and MR may be associated with an enlarged LV, and a disproportionately enlarged LV suggests severe MR, indicating refraining from moderate- or high-intensity sports. Asymptomatic individuals with mild or moderate MR may compete in all sports if they have good functional capacity, preserved LV function, sPAP <50 mmHg, and absence of complex arrhythmias during exercise. Individuals with symptomatic MR and reduced exercise capacity or MR with exercise-induced complex arrhythmias should not participate in competitive or leisure sports; however, low-intensity aerobic exercise is encouraged to improve functional capacity and well-being. Individuals on long-term anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation should avoid contact or collision sports.

content.narrative_summary: Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) is defined by >2 mm leaflet displacement and has a prevalence of 1–2.4%, generally benign with a 10-year mortality of 5%. High-risk features for SCD include myocardial fibrosis at the infero-basal wall and papillary muscles, mitral annular disjunction, T-wave inversion in inferior leads, and right bundle branch block morphology VAs. Asymptomatic patients with mild or moderate MR may exercise; those with severe MR but no high-risk markers may engage in low- to moderate-intensity sports if LV dimensions and pressures are acceptable. Symptomatic patients or those with high-risk features should avoid competitive exercise but may do low-intensity aerobic activity. Mitral stenosis (MS) is uncommon in the West but increasing with immigration; risk stratification for exercise in MS relies on detailed echocardiography and maximal exercise stress testing.

5.5.4 Exercise recommendations in individuals with dilated cardiomyopathy
content.narrative_summary:
Left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) is an unclassified cardiomyopathy marked by prominent trabeculation and deep recesses communicating with the LV cavity, presenting with progressive LV dysfunction, ventricular tachyarrhythmias, and thromboembolic events. Athletes may demonstrate hypertrabeculation; increased preload can unmask LV trabecular morphology. Evaluation should be limited to those meeting echocardiographic criteria plus LV systolic dysfunction, symptoms, or positive family history. Additional imaging criteria include a thin compacted layer (<5 mm end-diastole on CMR or <8 mm in systole) and abnormal myocardial relaxation (E′ <9 cm/s). Such athletes require further assessment with CMR, exercise echocardiography, and Holter monitoring to detect fibrosis, thrombi, contractile reserve, and exercise-induced arrhythmias.

Risk stratification in LVNC is driven by symptoms, severity of LV dysfunction, and ventricular arrhythmias; no adverse events have been reported in the absence of LV dysfunction regardless of trabeculation severity. Regular follow-up is recommended, with new symptoms prompting interruption of exercise and reevaluation.

Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is characterized by LV or biventricular systolic dysfunction not explained by loading conditions or CAD, with possible causes including genetic predisposition, myocarditis, toxins, peripartum cardiomyopathy, and in some cases multiple factors. The disease spectrum ranges from asymptomatic LV dilation with normal or low-normal systolic function to overt systolic dysfunction with limiting symptoms. Ventricular arrhythmias are common, especially with prior myocarditis or lamin A/C and filamin C mutations. Exercise training improves function and quality of life but intensive or competitive sports may increase SCD risk. content.narrative_summary: The section discusses the prognostic and symptomatic relevance of atrial fibrillation (AF) during sports, emphasizing exclusion of underlying structural heart disease, hyperthyroidism, alcohol or drug abuse, and temporary cessation of intense sports until causes are addressed. Rapid atrioventricular conduction during exercise can cause symptoms and mandates symptom‐guided exercise cessation and optimized rate control; prophylactic cavo-tricuspid isthmus ablation may be considered if atrial flutter is documented. Rate control with beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, or digitalis can be challenging, and class I or III antiarrhythmics carry risks and should not be used as monotherapy due to potential development of AFL. Oral anticoagulation decisions are based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, and direct trauma sports should be avoided on anticoagulation. Pulmonary vein isolation may be offered if drug therapy fails or as first-line in select patients, with similar outcomes in athletes and non-athletes. After successful ablation, if no AF recurs within 1 month, sports may resume, but no firm guidance exists on a ‘safe’ exercise dose post-ablation.

Counselling about the effect of long-lasting intense sports participation on (recurrence of) AF is recommended in individuals with AF who exercise vigorously for prolonged periods, especially in middle-aged men.
AF ablation is recommended in exercising individuals with recurrent symptomatic AF, and/or in those who do not want drug therapy, given its impact on athletic performance.
The ventricular rate while exercising with AF should be considered in every exercising individual (by symptoms and/or by ECG monitoring), and titrated rate control should be instituted.
Participation in sports without antiarrhythmic therapy should be considered in individuals without structural heart disease, and in whom AF is well tolerated.
Cavo-tricuspid isthmus ablation should be considered in those with documented flutter who want to engage in intensive exercise, to prevent atrial flutter 1:1 atrioventricular conduction.
Prophylactic cavo-tricuspid isthmus ablation to prevent flutter should be considered in individuals with AF who want to engage in intensive exercise and in whom class I drug therapy is initiated.
The use of class I antiarrhythmic drugs as monotherapy, without proof of adequate rate control of AF/AFL during vigorous exercise, is not recommended.
After ingestion of pill-in-the-pocket flecainide or propafenone, participation in intensive sports is not recommended until two half-lives of the antiarrhythmic drug have elapsed (i.e. up to 2 days).
Sports with direct bodily contact or prone to trauma are not recommended in exercising individuals with AF who are anticoagulated.

Participation in high-intensity recreational exercise/sports or any competitive sports is not recommended in individuals with ACM including those who are genotype positive and phenotype negative.

Participation in high-intensity exercise or competitive sports is not recommended in individuals with symptoms, LVEF<40% and/or frequent and/or complex VAs on ambulatory Holter monitoring or exercise testing.

Participation in high- or very high-intensity exercise including competitive sports is not recommended for individuals with a DCM and any of the following: (i) symptoms or history of cardiac arrest or unexplained syncope; (ii) LVEF<45%; (iii) frequent and/or complex VAs on ambulatory Holter monitoring or exercise testing; (iv) extensive LGE (>20%) on CMR; or (v) high-risk genotype (lamin A/C or filamin C).
Comprehensive evaluation, using imaging studies, exercise stress test, and Holter monitoring, is recommended following recovery from acute myocarditis to assess the risk of exercise-related SCD.

Return to all forms of exercise including competitive sports is recommended after 30 days to 3 months of rest for individuals who have recovered completely from acute pericarditis, depending on clinical severity.

Among individuals with a probable or definitive diagnosis of recent myocarditis or pericarditis, participation in leisure-time or competitive sports while active inflammation is present is not recommended.
Participation in moderate- to high-intensity exercise for a period of 3–6 months after acute myocarditis is not recommended.
Participation in moderate- to high-intensity exercise, including competitive sports, is not recommended for individuals with constrictive pericarditis.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents a comprehensive table of exercise recommendations for individuals with various arrhythmias and implantable cardiac devices, covering atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia with pre-excitation, premature ventricular contractions/non-sustained VT, long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, implanted electronic devices, congenital heart disease, and pregnancy.

recommendation_tables.title: Exercise recommendations in individuals with atrial fibrillation

rows.recommendation: Regular physical activity is recommended to prevent AF.
Evaluation and management of structural heart disease, thyroid dysfunction, alcohol or drug abuse, or other primary causes of AF is recommended before engaging in sports.
AF ablation is recommended in exercising individuals with recurrent, symptomatic AF and/or in those who do not want drug therapy, given its impact on athletic performance.
Sports with direct bodily contact or prone to trauma are not recommended in exercising individuals with AF who are anticoagulated.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for exercise and sports participation in individuals with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia and pre-excitation

rows.recommendation: In individuals with palpitations, a comprehensive assessment to exclude (latent) pre-excitation, structural heart disease, and VAs is recommended.
Ablation of the accessory pathway is recommended in competitive and recreational athletes with pre-excitation and documented arrhythmias.
In competitive/professional athletes with asymptomatic pre-excitation, an EP study is recommended to evaluate the risk for sudden death.

recommendation_tables.title: Exercise recommendations in individuals with premature ventricular contractions or non-sustained ventricular tachycardia

rows.recommendation: In exercising individuals with ≥2 PVCs on a baseline ECG (or ≥1 PVC in case of high-endurance athletes) a thorough evaluation (including a detailed family history) to exclude underlying structural or arrhythmogenic conditions is recommended.
Among individuals with frequent PVCs and non-sustained VT a thorough investigation with Holter monitoring, 12-lead ECG, exercise test, and suitable imaging is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Exercise recommendations in long QT syndrome

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that all exercising individuals with LQTS with prior symptoms or prolonged QTc be on therapy with beta-blockers at target dose.
It is recommended that exercising individuals with LQTS should avoid QT-prolonging drugs (www.crediblemeds.org) and electrolyte imbalance such as hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia.

Participation in high-intensity recreational and competitive sports, even when on beta-blockers, is not recommended in individuals with a QTc >500 ms or a genetically confirmed LQTS with a QTc ≥470 ms in males or ≥480 ms in females.
Participation in competitive sports (with or without ICD) is not recommended in individuals with LQTS and prior cardiac arrest or arrhythmic syncope.

recommendation_tables.title: Exercise recommendations in Brugada syndrome

rows.recommendation: ICD implantation is recommended in patients with BrS with episodes of arrhythmic syncope and/or aborted SCD.

Prescription of drugs that may aggravate BrS, electrolyte abnormalities, and sports practices that increase core temperature >39 °C are not recommended in individuals with overt BrS or phenotypically negative mutation carriers.

recommendation_tables.title: Exercise recommendations in individuals with implantable cardiac electronic devices

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that individuals with implanted devices with/without resynchronization and underlying disease follow the recommendations pertaining to the underlying disease.
An ICD is not recommended as a substitute for disease-related recommendations when these mandate sports restrictions.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for patients with congenital heart disease

rows.recommendation: Participation in regular moderate exercise is recommended in all individuals with CHD.
A discussion on exercise participation and provision of an individualized exercise prescription is recommended at every CHD patient encounter.
Competitive sport is not recommended for individuals with CHD who are in NYHA class III–IV or with potentially serious arrhythmias.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for exercise in pregnancy

rows.recommendation: Among pregnant women without medical or obstetric contraindications, participation in at least 150 min/week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise before, during, and after pregnancy is recommended.

Re-evaluation before continuing exercise or training is recommended in pregnant woman if they experience excessive shortness of breath, severe chest pain, dizziness or syncope, regular painful contractions, vaginal bleeding, or amniotic fluid leakage.

Among women with CVD who were habitually engaged in strength training or power sport disciplines before pregnancy, discussing the option with the medical team before continuing and avoiding the Valsalva manoeuvre is recommended.
Exercise or sport involving forceful physical contact, risk of falling or abdominal trauma, heavy lifting, scuba diving, or exercising at high altitude when unacclimatized are not recommended.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents exercise recommendations for various patient populations: pregnant individuals (continued from previous page), those with chronic kidney disease, cancer, spinal cord injury, ventricular assist devices, and peripheral arterial disease, each with specified Class of Recommendation (COR) and Level of Evidence (LOE). Footnotes list abbreviations. The page also includes links to supplementary data and begins the Appendix section listing author affiliations.

rows.recommendation: Vigorous exercise associated with a maximal predicted heart rate >90% of the predicted heart rate is not recommended during pregnancy.
Exercising while lying supine on a hard surface is not recommended after the first trimester due to the risk of decreased venous return and uterine blood flow.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for exercise in chronic kidney disease

rows.recommendation: Low- to moderate-intensity aerobic exercise training (up to 150 min/week), and low- to moderate-intensity resistance exercise training (2 day per week, 8–12 exercises, 12–15 repetitions), and flexibility exercises are recommended in all individuals with CKD.
Among patients with established osteodystrophy/osteoporosis, or coagulopathies, participation in contact sports is not recommended.

Participation in sport is not recommended in the following circumstances: electrolyte abnormalities, recent changes to the ECG, excess inter-dialysis weight gain, changing or titration of medication regimen, pulmonary congestion, and increasing peripheral oedema.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for exercise in individuals with cancer

rows.recommendation: Regular exercise during and after cancer therapy is recommended to reduce cancer-related fatigue, and improve quality of life, physical fitness, and prognosis.
Among individuals treated with cardiotoxic medications, echocardiography before participation in high-intensity exercise is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for exercise in individuals with spinal cord injury

rows.recommendation: In adults with spinal cord injury participation in 20 min of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise at least 3 times a week, along with moderate-intensity resistance training 2–3 times per week, is recommended for cardiorespiratory fitness, cardiometabolic health, and muscle strength benefits.

Artificial methods of inducing autonomic dysreflexia by causing intentional pain to the lower half of the body (‘boosting’) through obstruction of an indwelling urinary catheter, overly tight leg straps and electrical shocks or other methods of pain to the genitalia or lower limbs can be life-threatening and are not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for exercise in individuals with ventricular assist devices

rows.recommendation: Regular exercise, through cardiac rehabilitation, combining moderate-intensity aerobic and resistance exercise, is recommended in individuals with a ventricular assist device (VAD).
Sports that may potentially affect any of the VAD components (e.g. with body contact) are not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Physical activity and sports recommendations in patients and athletes with peripheral arterial disease

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that patients with atherosclerotic PAD perform regular exercise (at least 150 min/week of moderate aerobic exercise or 75 min/week of vigorous aerobic exercise or a combination thereof) as part of the secondary prevention strategy.
In patients with symptomatic LEAD, supervised exercise training programmes including walking to the maximal or submaximal distance for at least 3 h/week are indicated.
Continuation of competitive sports is recommended in athletes with traumatic or non-traumatic PAD following recovery after successful open surgery or percutaneous revascularization.
